topics.title: The hook: 6 agents became 7
topics.why_now: Your last video on this channel said 6 agents work inside this graph. The build step has been rebuilt since, and the first real livestream went through it on Nov 18.
topics.angle: Open on the number, then promise the code. Engineer to engineer: what changed, why, and the lines that do it.

prompts: In my last video I told you 6 agents work inside this graph. It's 7 now. And the step that builds each short went from one agent to four steps.
I'll show you why I split it, the code that does it, and what happened the first time a real livestream ran through it.
One livestream took 44 agent runs. Let me show you where they all come from.

topics.title: What changed: one agent became four steps
topics.why_now: The whole update is one node of the graph: the step that builds each short.
topics.angle: Show the before and the after on one slide before any code, so every code tab has a map to hang on.

tabs.label: One Agent Became Four Steps
prompts: Before, one agent did everything for a short. It planned the images, generated them in a browser, checked its own images, and built the video.
Now that's four steps. The builder plans. A second agent generates the images. A third agent checks them. Then the builder comes back and builds.
Same builder, called twice. And it never touches the browser anymore.

facts.text: Per short it is now 4 steps and 3 agents: plan (remotion-builder), images (image-gen), image check (visual-qa), build (remotion-builder again)
facts.source: batch_graph.py, the comment above the build pipeline

facts.text: A rejected image goes back to image-gen with the checker's report, 2 rounds at most

careful: Only the build step changed. Picking the clips, cutting, tightening and publishing work the way your last video showed them.

topics.title: Why I split it
topics.why_now: Each of the three reasons is something that went wrong, or could not be checked, in the one-agent build.
topics.angle: Three concrete problems, then the rule that came out of them: one agent per decision, and code where nothing is being decided.

tabs.label: Three Problems With One Agent Doing It All
prompts: Three things pushed me to split it. One: there's a single browser making the images, so a builder had to wait its turn. And once, an agent ended its turn while it was waiting. The run sat there.
Two: the only one checking the images was the agent that made them.
Three: generating images is mechanical work, and it was running on the big model I use to write the video code.
So here's the rule I use now. One agent per decision. And if nothing is being decided, it shouldn't be an agent. It should be code.

facts.text: The builder that quit: batch archie-promo, Sep 24, 2026. It saw the image generator queued behind another builder, said "I'll continue when it finishes", and its process exited with the short unbuilt
facts.source: .claude/agents/remotion-builder.md, the section "Never end your turn to wait"

facts.text: remotion-builder runs on opus at xhigh effort. image-gen runs on sonnet at xhigh effort
facts.source: the model and effort lines of the two agent definitions

careful: Put no number on money or time saved. The old build and the new one were never timed against each other.

topics.title: The names for this
topics.why_now: These patterns have standard names, and an interviewer will know them.
topics.angle: Tie your build step to the industry's words once, so nobody takes it for a private invention: a workflow, prompt chaining with a gate, and the evaluator-optimizer loop.

tabs.label: Anthropic: Building effective agents
tabs.show: Scroll to the heading "Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer", the last of the five workflows.
highlights: Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths.
one LLM call generates a response while another provides evaluation and feedback
prompts: None of this is my invention, and it has names. Anthropic calls a system where code decides the order a workflow. That's my graph: code picks the next step, and each step is an agent.
One model generates and another one evaluates, in a loop. They call that evaluator-optimizer. Mine is the same pattern with whole agents, and I cap it at two rounds.
And plan first, check, then build: that's prompt chaining with a gate in the middle.

facts.text: Anthropic, "Building effective agents", published Dec 19, 2024. It names 5 workflows: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer
Its prompt chaining section says you can add programmatic checks, which it calls a gate, on the steps in between

careful: The article describes single LLM calls. Yours are whole agents, so say "the same pattern", never "what Anthropic built".
The page says at its top that much of the tooling it describes has changed since December 2024. You are borrowing its pattern names, nothing about tools.

topics.title: The code: five changes
topics.why_now: 5 files changed. These are the five places worth putting on screen.
topics.angle: Open each file at the line and say what was added. The first three are the Python. The last two are the agents' own instructions.

tabs.label: batch_graph.py: _build_clip, the whole pipeline in 17 lines
tabs.show: Start on the def. The three calls are lines 1088, 1092 and 1093.
prompts: This is the whole thing. Plan. Images and the check. Build. Three calls.
Look at the if on top. If the plan files are already on disk, it skips the plan. Every step works that way, so when a run dies halfway I run it again and it picks up where it stopped.
And the graph never takes the agent's word for it. After the plan stage, it checks that the two files are really on disk.

facts.text: Added: _build_clip, lines 1080 to 1096. The plan stage is line 1088, the images and the check are line 1092, the build stage is line 1093
The skip: line 1087 runs the plan stage only when BROLL-PLAN.md or a valid image list is missing. Line 1089 checks again after the agent returns
Changed: lane2_build maps _build_clip over the clips on line 1156, 3 at a time on this run. Before, that line started one builder per clip

tabs.label: batch_graph.py: _clip_images, the lock and the check loop
tabs.show: The lock is lines 1046 to 1052. The loop starts on line 1042.
prompts: The browser makes one image at a time, so there's a lock around it. Before, the agent had to take that lock itself. Now the code takes it, starts the agent, and releases it in a finally block.
An agent can stop while it's waiting for a lock. A finally block can't.
Then the loop. Generate, check, and if the checker rejects something, go around once more with the checker's report. Two rounds, then it stops and the builder gets a note.

facts.text: The lock: taken on line 1046, image-gen started on line 1049, released in finally on line 1052
The loop: line 1042. visual-qa starts on line 1058, and _qa_verdict (line 1010) reads the last line of its answer, VERDICT: PASS or VERDICT: FAIL
visual-qa has no Write tool, so the graph saves its report itself on line 1063. The round limit is BROLL_QA_ROUNDS = 2, line 875

careful: The standard word for this lock is a mutex. Yours is a small script the graph calls, not a LangGraph feature, so don't present it as one.

tabs.label: batch_graph.py: one agent, two prompts
tabs.show: The plan prompt starts on line 912. Jump to line 980 for the build prompt.
prompts: I didn't write a planner agent. It's the same builder with two prompts. Stage 1 of 2: plan only, write two files, stop. Stage 2 of 2: the images are done, build from what's on disk.
Those two files are the handoff. A plan a person can read, and a JSON list for the next agent: one object per image, with the file path and the full prompt.
And code validates that JSON before the image agent ever starts.

facts.text: Added: _plan_prompt, lines 912 to 930, with "STAGE 1 of 2 (PLAN ONLY)" on line 915. Rewritten: _build_prompt, lines 980 to 997, with "STAGE 2 of 2 (BUILD)" on line 983
Added: broll_items, line 894, validates the list. Every item needs a prompt and an absolute .png path, and an empty list is valid
Added: the prompts for the other two agents, _images_prompt on line 933 and _broll_qa_prompt on line 963

topics.title: What the independent check caught
topics.why_now: The run produced real catches, and the rejected images were kept on disk.
topics.angle: This is the proof for the second reason. Show the pictures and let them make the point.

tabs.label: What The Image Check Caught
prompts: This is why the checker is its own agent. On the left, what the image model made. On the right, after the checker sent it back.
The prompt said put only the coin's own mark on it. The model drew a little face next to the mark. The checker rejected it, wrote the fix for the prompt, and the retry came back clean.
Same thing with the cat. The model gave the mascot a satchel and a bedroll nobody asked for, in all 5 images of that short.

facts.text: Clip 6, round 1: "the cat wears a satchel and bedroll that are in neither the prompt nor the reference", in all 5 images
facts.source: the checker's report in the graph's log

facts.text: Clip 3, round 1: a made-up brand label on a tool's battery, around 20 by 60 pixels. Regenerated, and it passed in round 2

topics.title: What I'd change next, and the close
topics.why_now: The run also showed two limits, and the fix for one of them is already clear.
topics.angle: End as an engineer: what the numbers told you, the next change, then the one rule to take away.

prompts: Two things the run taught me. The browser is the bottleneck. The build took 4 hours and 38 minutes, and the browser was busy for around 3.9 of those hours.

And a retry fixes content. It doesn't fix framing. When the checker said the subject sits too close to the edge, regenerating never fixed it. So framing problems will go to the builder as a crop, and only content problems go back to the image agent.
If you take one thing from this video: when one agent is making two different decisions, split it. And when nothing is being decided, write code.
If you haven't seen the first video on this graph, watch that one next.
